why: Every finance job, from FP&A to audit, credit or equity research, starts with the same three statements. Hiring managers expect a junior analyst to read an income statement, a balance sheet and a cash flow statement, explain how they link, and say in two minutes whether a company is healthy.
outcome: record transactions with double entry and accruals, read and build the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, walk a transaction through all three, measure working capital (DSO, DIO, DPO, cash conversion cycle) and compute the ratios an analyst reads first, in Excel.

lessons.title: What a financial analyst does and the accounting equation
text: A financial analyst turns accounting numbers into decisions. In a company (FP&A, controlling) the job is budgets, forecasts, monthly reporting and explaining why actuals differ from plan. In a bank or a fund (credit, equity research, M&A) it is judging whether a company can repay a loan or is worth its price. Both start from the same raw material: the financial statements, built by accountants from thousands of individual transactions.

Everything in accounting rests on one identity: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are the resources the company controls and expects to bring future benefits (cash, receivables, stock, machines). Liabilities are what it owes to outsiders (suppliers, banks, tax authorities, customers who paid in advance). Equity is what is left for the owners: the money they put in plus the profits kept in the business. The two sides always balance because every resource was financed by someone, either a creditor or an owner.

Each transaction changes at least two items and keeps the equation true. A bank loan of 50 raises cash (an asset) and borrowings (a liability) by 50. Buying a machine for 60 in cash swaps one asset for another. A profitable sale raises cash and, through profit, raises equity. Following the equation line by line is the fastest way to check your understanding of any transaction, and interviewers often ask exactly that.

Companies publish three main statements. The income statement (profit and loss, P&L) shows performance over a period. The balance sheet (statement of financial position under IFRS) is a photo of what the company owns and owes on one date. The cash flow statement explains how cash moved over the period. Listed companies in the EU report under IFRS; US companies use US GAAP. The logic is the same, some rules and names differ, and the course points them out.

In the first weeks of a finance job you will mostly reconcile numbers: check that the balance sheet balances, that the cash in the statements equals the bank, that this month’s figures tie to last month’s. Being rigorous with small numbers is what builds trust before anyone lets you present a recommendation.
points: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, always, after every transaction.
Equity = capital put in by the owners + retained earnings (profits not paid out).
Income statement: a period. Balance sheet: one date. Cash flow statement: a period.
IFRS (EU listed groups, most of the world) and US GAAP: same logic, different rules and names.
An analyst explains numbers and their causes, not just reports them.

example.code:
Transaction                          Assets                    = Liabilities + Equity
Owners put in 100 in cash            cash 100                  = 0           + 100
Bank loan of 50                      cash 150                  = 50          + 100
Buy a machine for 60 in cash         cash 90, machine 60       = 50          + 100
Services sold 40, costs 25, in cash  cash 105, machine 60      = 50          + 115
example.note: After each line both sides are equal: 165 = 50 + 115 at the end. The profit of 15 is the increase in equity.

lessons.title: Double entry, accruals and the accounting period
text: Double entry records every transaction as at least one debit and one credit of the same total. Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity and revenue. The words come from Latin and mean nothing like “good” or “bad”: a debit to cash is money coming in. Because total debits always equal total credits, the trial balance (the list of every account’s balance) must sum to zero, which is the first control at each month-end close.

Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, not when cash moves. A consultancy that finishes a 1,200 job in March and is paid in April shows the revenue in March, with a trade receivable until the cash arrives. March rent invoiced in April is still a March expense: the accountant books an accrued expense (a liability) at the end of March. An insurance premium of 1,200 paid in January for the year is a prepaid expense (an asset) released at 100 a month. Cash accounting would make every month swing with the timing of payments; accruals make periods comparable.

Revenue recognition is where most judgement sits. Under IFRS 15 (and its US twin, ASC 606) revenue follows five steps: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations (the distinct promises), determine the transaction price, allocate it to the obligations, and recognise revenue when or as each obligation is satisfied. A software company that sells a 1,200 annual subscription paid upfront records the cash and a contract liability (deferred revenue) of 1,200, then recognises 100 of revenue each month as it delivers the service.

The accounting period is usually a month for internal reporting and a quarter or a year for published accounts. Cut-off is the discipline of putting each transaction in the right period: a delivery made on 31 December belongs to that year, one made on 2 January to the next. Many audit findings and restatements are cut-off errors, often under pressure to “pull” sales into a good quarter.

Expect interview questions such as “Where does a customer prepayment go?” (a liability, deferred revenue, until the service is delivered) or “What is an accrual?” Answer with the entry and its effect on the statements, not just a definition.
points: Debit: increases assets and expenses. Credit: increases liabilities, equity and revenue.
Total debits = total credits, so the trial balance sums to zero.
Accrued expense: cost of the period not yet invoiced (liability). Prepaid expense: paid in advance (asset).
Deferred revenue (contract liability): cash received before the service is delivered.
IFRS 15 / ASC 606: revenue when or as each performance obligation is satisfied.

example.code:
Date    Entry                                         Debit   Credit
15 Mar  Trade receivables / Revenue                   1,200   1,200
31 Mar  Rent expense / Accrued expenses                 500     500
15 Apr  Cash / Trade receivables                      1,200   1,200
1 Jan   Cash / Deferred revenue (annual subscription) 1,200   1,200
31 Jan  Deferred revenue / Revenue (one month)          100     100
example.note: The first account of each line is debited, the second credited. Revenue is earned when the work is done; cash only moves the receivable.

lessons.title: The income statement: from revenue to net income
text: The income statement reads from top to bottom, subtracting costs in layers. Revenue (sales, turnover) minus cost of sales (what it cost to make or buy what was sold) gives gross profit. Operating expenses (selling, general and administrative costs, research) bring you to operating profit, often called EBIT (earnings before interest and tax). Net finance costs (interest paid minus interest earned) give profit before tax, and income tax leaves net income, the profit attributable to the owners.

EBITDA adds depreciation and amortisation back to EBIT: EBITDA = EBIT + D&A. Depreciation spreads the cost of a machine over its useful life; amortisation does the same for intangible assets such as software or licences. Neither is a cash payment in the year, so EBITDA is used as a rough proxy for operating cash generation and is the base of many debt covenants (net debt / EBITDA). It is not a cash measure, though: it ignores capex, working capital, interest and tax, and it is not defined by IFRS or US GAAP, so each company computes its own version.

Margins divide each level of profit by revenue so that companies and periods can be compared: gross margin, EBITDA margin, EBIT margin (operating margin), net margin. In the example, a 40 % gross margin and a 15 % EBIT margin say that the product is priced well above its direct cost, and that overheads eat 25 points of revenue. Analysts care more about the trend and the comparison with peers than about one number.

Costs can be presented by function (cost of sales, selling, administrative, as most groups do) or by nature (purchases, staff costs, depreciation, as many French companies do). IFRS allows both; US GAAP income statements are almost always by function. IFRS 18, which replaces IAS 1 for periods from 2027, adds required subtotals such as operating profit and asks companies to explain the “management-defined performance measures” (like adjusted EBITDA) they publish.

Watch for one-off items: restructuring costs, impairments, gains on disposals. Companies often show an “adjusted” or “recurring” profit without them. Use it, but always reconcile it to the reported figure and ask whether the one-offs really happen only once.
points: Revenue − cost of sales = gross profit; − operating expenses = EBIT; − net finance costs − tax = net income.
EBITDA = EBIT + depreciation and amortisation (D&A). Not a cash flow, not a standard measure.
Margin = profit level / revenue: gross margin, EBITDA margin, EBIT margin, net margin.
Presentation by function or by nature: same profit, different lines.
Reconcile adjusted profit to reported profit before using it.

example.code:
Revenue                             1,000
Cost of sales                        (600)
Gross profit                          400   40.0 %
Operating expenses (SG&A, R&D)       (250)   incl. D&A of 50
EBIT (operating profit)               150   15.0 %
Net finance costs                     (30)
Profit before tax                     120
Income tax (25 %)                     (30)
Net income                             90    9.0 %

EBITDA = EBIT + D&A = 150 + 50 =     200   20.0 %
example.note: Each margin is the profit line divided by revenue of 1,000. D&A sits inside the cost lines, so EBITDA is computed, not read.

lessons.title: The balance sheet: assets, liabilities and equity
text: The balance sheet lists what the company controls (assets) and how it is financed (liabilities and equity) at the closing date. Items are split between current (expected to be settled or used within twelve months or the operating cycle) and non-current. Current assets are inventories, trade receivables, prepaid expenses and cash; non-current assets are property, plant and equipment (PP&E), intangible assets, goodwill, right-of-use assets and long-term investments.

Liabilities follow the same split: trade payables, accrued expenses, deferred revenue, tax payable and the part of borrowings due within a year are current; long-term borrowings, lease liabilities, provisions and pensions are non-current. Equity holds share capital, share premium and retained earnings (the accumulated profits not paid as dividends), plus some reserves. Retained earnings are the link with the income statement: each year they grow by net income and fall by dividends.

IFRS and US GAAP name and order things differently. IFRS calls it the statement of financial position and many European groups list non-current assets first and end with liabilities; US GAAP balance sheets list current assets first, in order of liquidity. IFRS says “inventories”, “trade receivables”, “share capital” and “retained earnings”; US GAAP says “inventory”, “accounts receivable”, “common stock” and “retained earnings” too. Under IFRS 16 almost every lease appears on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability; US GAAP (ASC 842) also brings leases on the balance sheet but keeps a straight-line rent expense for operating leases.

Most assets are at historical cost less depreciation, not at market value. Goodwill (the premium paid in an acquisition over the fair value of the net assets bought) is not amortised under IFRS or US GAAP for public companies but tested for impairment every year. A large goodwill balance means the company grew by acquisitions, and an impairment means it overpaid.

Analysts read the balance sheet for three things: liquidity (can it pay what is due soon?), leverage (how much debt compared with equity and profit?) and the capital tied up in the business (working capital and fixed assets). Net debt (borrowings plus lease liabilities minus cash) is the figure bankers start from; always say whether you include leases.
points: Current: settled or used within 12 months. Non-current: longer.
Retained earnings rise with net income and fall with dividends: the link to the P&L.
IFRS “statement of financial position”, “trade receivables”; US GAAP “balance sheet”, “accounts receivable”.
Leases are on the balance sheet (IFRS 16, ASC 842): right-of-use asset + lease liability.
Net debt = borrowings + lease liabilities − cash (say whether leases are in).

example.code:
ASSETS                               EQUITY AND LIABILITIES
Property, plant and equipment  500   Share capital                100
Intangible assets              120   Retained earnings            400
Goodwill                        80   Total equity                 500
Non-current assets             700   Borrowings (long-term)       340
Inventories                    150   Lease liabilities             60
Trade receivables              200   Non-current liabilities      400
Cash                            90   Trade payables               160
Current assets                 440   Short-term borrowings         50
                                     Accrued expenses              30
                                     Current liabilities          240
Total assets                 1,140   Total equity and liabilities 1,140
example.note: Both sides equal 1,140. Net debt including leases = 340 + 50 + 60 − 90 = 360.

lessons.title: The cash flow statement: why profit is not cash
text: The cash flow statement explains the change in cash over the period in three sections. Operating activities: cash generated by the business itself. Investing activities: cash spent on or received from long-term assets (capital expenditure, acquisitions, disposals). Financing activities: cash from or to lenders and owners (new borrowings, repayments, share issues, dividends). The total equals the change in cash on the balance sheet, which is the first check an analyst makes.

Almost every company presents operating cash flow with the indirect method: start from net income, add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortisation, impairments), then adjust for changes in working capital. An increase in receivables or inventories uses cash (subtract it); an increase in payables or deferred revenue provides cash (add it). The direct method lists cash received from customers and paid to suppliers; IFRS and US GAAP encourage it but few companies use it.

Profit and cash differ for three main reasons. Non-cash costs reduce profit but not cash (depreciation). Working capital: a sale on 60-day credit is revenue today and cash in two months, so a fast-growing company can show profits and run out of cash. Capital expenditure is cash out today but reaches profit only through depreciation over many years. This is why lenders and investors look at cash flow, and why “profitable but bankrupt” is a classic interview question.

Free cash flow is the cash left after keeping the business running and growing: in its simplest form, operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. Definitions vary (some deduct lease payments and interest), so state the one you use. In the example, the company earns 90 of net income but its free cash flow is negative (−25) because it is investing heavily and its receivables grew.

Classification differs between frameworks. Under US GAAP interest paid is an operating cash flow and dividends paid are financing. IAS 7 today lets IFRS companies choose; IFRS 18 removes most of this choice from 2027 (interest and dividends paid in financing for most companies). When you compare two companies, check where they put interest, otherwise their operating cash flows are not comparable. IFRS 18 also makes operating profit, rather than net income, the starting point of the indirect method.
points: Three sections: operating, investing, financing; total = change in cash.
Indirect method: net income + D&A − increase in working capital.
Receivables or inventories up: cash down. Payables or deferred revenue up: cash up.
Free cash flow ≈ operating cash flow − capex (state your definition).
Interest paid: operating under US GAAP, a choice under IFRS until IFRS 18.

example.code:
Net income                                   90
Depreciation and amortisation                50
Increase in trade receivables               (40)
Increase in inventories                     (20)
Increase in trade payables                   15
Cash flow from operating activities          95
Capital expenditure                        (120)
Cash flow from investing activities        (120)
New borrowings                               40
Dividends paid                              (20)
Cash flow from financing activities          20
Net change in cash                           (5)

Free cash flow = 95 − 120 =                 (25)
example.note: Profit of 90, yet cash falls by 5: growth in receivables and stock plus heavy investment.

lessons.title: How the three statements link
text: The three statements are one system. Net income from the income statement is the first line of the cash flow statement and flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet. The cash flow statement ends with the change in cash, which must equal the movement of cash between the opening and the closing balance sheets. Depreciation reduces PP&E on the balance sheet, reduces profit on the income statement and is added back in the cash flow statement. If any of these links breaks, the model or the accounts contain an error.

The classic interview question is: “Depreciation goes up by 10. Walk me through the three statements.” With a 25 % tax rate: on the income statement, EBIT falls by 10, tax falls by 2.5, net income falls by 7.5. On the cash flow statement, net income is down 7.5 but depreciation of 10 is added back, so operating cash flow rises by 2.5 (the tax saved). On the balance sheet, PP&E falls by 10 and cash rises by 2.5, so assets fall by 7.5; retained earnings fall by 7.5, so equity falls by 7.5. Both sides fall by 7.5: it balances.

Use the same method for any transaction: start with the income statement (is there revenue or an expense?), then the cash flow statement (did cash move, in which section?), then the balance sheet (which assets and liabilities changed?), and finish by checking that assets still equal liabilities plus equity. Buying inventory for cash changes no profit: cash down, inventory up. Selling that inventory on credit creates revenue and cost of sales, raises receivables and lowers inventory, but cash does not move until the customer pays.

In a three-statement model built in Excel, the balance check (total assets minus total liabilities and equity) sits at the bottom of each year and must be zero. When it is not, the usual causes are a cash flow line that has no balance sheet counterpart, a sign error (an increase in receivables added instead of subtracted), or a dividend booked in the income statement instead of equity.

Learn three walk-throughs by heart (depreciation up 10, inventory bought on credit, a debt-financed machine) and practise saying them in under a minute: interviewers check both the logic and the order you present it in.
points: Net income → top of the cash flow statement and into retained earnings.
Change in cash on the cash flow statement = change in cash on the balance sheet.
Depreciation +10 at 25 % tax: net income −7.5, cash +2.5, PP&E −10, equity −7.5.
Method: income statement, then cash flow, then balance sheet, then check it balances.
A model’s balance check must be zero every period.

example.code:
Depreciation +10, tax rate 25 %

Income statement      EBIT −10   tax −2.5   net income −7.5
Cash flow statement   net income −7.5   + depreciation 10   = cash +2.5
Balance sheet         PP&E −10   cash +2.5   => assets −7.5
                      retained earnings −7.5 => equity −7.5
Check                 −7.5 = −7.5
example.note: The only real cash effect is the tax saving: 10 × 25 % = 2.5.

lessons.title: Working capital and the cash conversion cycle
text: Operating working capital is the cash tied up in the day-to-day cycle: trade receivables plus inventories minus trade payables (some definitions add other operating items such as deferred revenue). A company pays suppliers, holds stock, sells on credit and waits to be paid; the longer that loop, the more cash it needs. That is why working capital is the first lever of a cash plan and why controllers chase it at every month-end.

Three ratios turn balances into days. DSO (days sales outstanding) = trade receivables / revenue × 365: how long customers take to pay. DIO (days inventory outstanding) = inventories / cost of sales × 365: how long goods stay in stock. DPO (days payables outstanding) = trade payables / cost of sales × 365: how long the company takes to pay its suppliers. Inventories and payables are compared with cost of sales, not revenue, because they are valued at cost.

The cash conversion cycle (CCC) = DSO + DIO − DPO: the number of days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. With revenue of 7,300, cost of sales of 4,380, receivables of 1,200, inventories of 720 and payables of 540, DSO is 60 days, DIO 60 days, DPO 45 days and the cycle 75 days. Each day of DSO here is worth 7,300 / 365 = 20 of cash: cutting DSO by 5 days frees 100.

Read the days with the business model. Supermarkets often have a negative cycle: customers pay at the till, stock turns fast and suppliers are paid later, so growth generates cash. Industrial companies with long projects carry high inventories and receivables. In France, payment terms between companies are capped by law (generally 60 days from the invoice date, or 45 days end of month), so a DSO far above that is a warning on collection.

Common traps: year-end balances can be window-dressed (a big collection push on 31 December), seasonal businesses need average balances, and factoring (selling receivables to a bank) lowers DSO without improving the business. When DSO jumps, ask whether one large customer is late, whether terms were extended to win sales, or whether revenue was recognised too early.
points: Operating working capital = trade receivables + inventories − trade payables.
DSO = receivables / revenue × 365; DIO = inventories / cost of sales × 365; DPO = payables / cost of sales × 365.
Cash conversion cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO.
One day of DSO is worth revenue / 365 of cash.
Use average balances for seasonal businesses; watch for factoring and window dressing.

example.note: With revenue in B2 (7,300), cost of sales in B3 (4,380), receivables in B4 (1,200), inventories in B5 (720), payables in B6 (540), and the results in D2:D5: DSO 60, DIO 60, DPO 45, cash conversion cycle 75 days.

lessons.title: Ratio analysis and reading an annual report
text: Ratios make statements comparable across years and companies. Group them in four families. Profitability: gross, EBITDA, EBIT and net margins. Liquidity: current ratio (current assets / current liabilities) and quick ratio ((current assets − inventories) / current liabilities). Leverage: net debt / EBITDA, debt / equity and interest cover (EBIT / net finance costs). Returns: ROE (net income / average equity) and ROCE (EBIT / capital employed, where capital employed = total assets − current liabilities, or equity + net debt).

Using the course’s income statement and balance sheet: EBIT margin 15 %, net margin 9 %, current ratio 440 / 240 = 1.83, quick ratio 290 / 240 = 1.21, net debt / EBITDA 360 / 200 = 1.8x, interest cover 150 / 30 = 5.0x, ROE 90 / 500 = 18 % on closing equity and ROCE 150 / 900 = 16.7 %. None of these numbers means anything alone: compare with the previous years, with peers and with the covenants in the loan agreements.

The DuPont breakdown explains where ROE comes from: ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier, that is (net income / revenue) × (revenue / total assets) × (total assets / equity). Here 9 % × 0.877 × 2.28 = 18 %. A high ROE can come from good margins, from using assets intensively, or simply from debt; ROCE, which ignores how the company is financed, tells you whether the business itself earns more than its cost of capital.

Read an annual report (in France, the document d’enregistrement universel of listed groups; in the US, the 10-K) in a fixed order: the auditor’s report (any qualification or key audit matter?), the three statements, then the notes, which hold the real information: accounting policies, revenue by segment, debt maturities, leases, provisions, off-balance-sheet commitments. Then read management’s commentary with the numbers in front of you and reconcile every alternative performance measure.

In a case interview, structure beats speed: state the trend in revenue and margins, then cash conversion (operating cash flow / EBITDA), then leverage and liquidity, then returns, and finish with two or three questions you would ask management. That is what a credit committee or an investment memo looks like.
points: Profitability: margins. Liquidity: current and quick ratios. Leverage: net debt / EBITDA, interest cover. Returns: ROE, ROCE.
ROE = net income / average equity; ROCE = EBIT / capital employed.
DuPont: ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier.
Compare with past years, peers and covenants; a ratio alone says little.
Annual report: auditor’s report, statements, notes, then management commentary.

example.code:
Ratio                  Formula                                   Value
EBIT margin            EBIT / revenue = 150 / 1,000              15.0 %
Net margin             net income / revenue = 90 / 1,000          9.0 %
Current ratio          current assets / current liab. = 440 / 240  1.83
Quick ratio            (440 − 150) / 240                           1.21
Net debt / EBITDA      360 / 200                                   1.8x
Interest cover         EBIT / net finance costs = 150 / 30         5.0x
ROE                    net income / equity = 90 / 500             18.0 %
ROCE                   EBIT / (total assets − current liab.)      16.7 %
                       = 150 / (1,140 − 240)
DuPont                 9.0 % × 0.877 × 2.28                       18.0 %
example.note: ROE here uses closing equity because only one balance sheet is shown; with two years, use the average.

lessons.title: French-style financial analysis: SIG, EBE, CAF and the functional balance sheet
text: Most French companies, SMEs and the subsidiaries of large groups alike, publish their individual accounts (comptes sociaux) under the French chart of accounts, the Plan comptable général (PCG), and file them with the tax return (the liasse fiscale, the 2050 series of forms); IFRS applies to the consolidated accounts of listed groups. The PCG income statement classifies costs by nature (purchases, external charges, staff, depreciation) rather than by function (cost of sales, SG&A), and French banks, auditors and contrôle de gestion teams analyse it with their own toolkit. “Analyste financier” and “contrôleur de gestion” offers ask for exactly that: SIG, EBE, CAF, FR, BFR. This lesson takes the course’s company (revenue 1,000, EBIT 150, net income 90) and reads it the French way.

The soldes intermédiaires de gestion (SIG, intermediate management balances) cut the income statement into a cascade of subtotals. Marge commerciale (trading margin) = sales of goods bought for resale − their cost (purchases ± change in stock). Production de l’exercice (output for the year) = production sold + production stockée (change in finished goods inventory) + production immobilisée (assets the company built for itself). Valeur ajoutée (value added) = trading margin + output − consommations en provenance de tiers (external consumption: raw materials, subcontracting, rent, energy, fees). Value added is the wealth the company creates and then shares between staff, the State, lenders, shareholders and reinvestment. Here: 160 + 600 − 340 = 420.

Excédent brut d’exploitation (EBE, gross operating surplus) = value added + operating subsidies − taxes other than income tax (impôts et taxes) − personnel costs: 420 − 20 − 200 = 200. Then résultat d’exploitation (≈ EBIT) = EBE − depreciation and provisions + write-backs ± other operating items = 150; résultat courant avant impôts (RCAI) = operating result ± résultat financier = 120; résultat exceptionnel holds unusual items (the 2025 PCG reform, ANC regulation 2022-06, made this category much narrower); résultat net = RCAI ± exceptional − participation des salariés (statutory employee profit-sharing) − corporate income tax = 90. EBE is close to EBITDA but not the same: EBE is defined by the PCG and stops before provisions and other operating income and charges, while EBITDA is a company-defined measure, usually EBIT + D&A. Under IFRS 16, rent leaves EBITDA (it becomes depreciation and interest), whereas in French individual accounts rent stays an external charge inside EBE, so a group’s IFRS EBITDA is often higher than the sum of its subsidiaries’ EBE.

Capacité d’autofinancement (CAF, internally generated funds) is the cash the year’s operations can generate before any change in working capital. Additive method, from net income: CAF = net income + depreciation, impairment and provisions charged − write-backs − proceeds from asset disposals + net book value of assets sold − investment subsidies released to income. Subtractive method, from EBE: CAF = EBE ± other operating income and charges paid in cash ± financial result paid in cash ± exceptional cash items (excluding disposals) − employee profit-sharing − income tax. Both give 140 here (90 + 50, or 200 − 30 − 30). CAF is not a cash flow: operating cash flow = CAF − increase in BFR, and autofinancement = CAF − dividends paid. Banks read debt repayment capacity as financial debt / CAF, in years.

The functional balance sheet (bilan fonctionnel) regroups the balance sheet by role rather than by maturity. Ressources stables (equity, depreciation and provisions, long-term debt) finance emplois stables (fixed assets at gross value); the surplus is the fonds de roulement net global (FRNG, net working capital in the long-term sense). The besoin en fonds de roulement (BFR, working capital requirement) = inventories + operating receivables − operating payables, split into BFR d’exploitation and hors exploitation. Trésorerie nette = cash − bank overdrafts and short-term bank lines, and the identity FRNG − BFR = trésorerie nette always holds. On the course’s balance sheet: FRNG = (500 + 340 + 60) − 700 = 200, BFR = (150 + 200) − (160 + 30) = 160, trésorerie nette = 40, which is cash 90 − short-term borrowings 50. Usual French ratios: EBE / revenue (taux de marge d’EBE), value added / revenue, personnel costs / value added, CAF / revenue, financial debt / CAF, BFR in days of revenue (BFR / revenue × 360, the French convention) and stable resources / stable uses.
points: SIG cascade: marge commerciale, production de l’exercice, valeur ajoutée, EBE, résultat d’exploitation, RCAI, résultat exceptionnel, résultat net.
EBE = value added + operating subsidies − taxes − personnel costs; close to EBITDA, but defined by the PCG and not affected by IFRS 16.
CAF additive = net income + charges not paid in cash − write-backs − disposal proceeds + NBV of assets sold; it ignores the change in BFR.
FRNG = stable resources − stable uses; BFR = inventories + operating receivables − operating payables.
Trésorerie nette = FRNG − BFR = cash − bank overdrafts: check it both ways.

− Coût d'achat des marchandises vendues                     (240)
= Marge commerciale (trading margin)                         160
Production vendue + stockée + immobilisée                    600
= Production de l'exercice (output for the year)             600
− Consommations en provenance de tiers (external)           (340)
= Valeur ajoutée (value added)                               420
+ Subventions d'exploitation − impôts et taxes               (20)
− Charges de personnel                                      (200)
= EBE (excédent brut d'exploitation)                         200
− Dotations aux amortissements et provisions                 (50)
= Résultat d'exploitation (≈ EBIT)                           150

pitfalls: Treating EBITDA as cash: it ignores capex, working capital, interest and tax.
Computing DIO or DPO on revenue instead of cost of sales.
Comparing operating cash flows of an IFRS and a US GAAP company without checking where interest paid is classified.
Quoting net debt without saying whether lease liabilities are included.
Using an “adjusted” profit without reconciling it to the reported figure.
Reading one year’s ratios alone, with no trend, no peers and no covenant to compare with.
Forgetting the tax effect when walking a transaction through the three statements.
Calling EBE and EBITDA the same number without reconciling leases (IFRS 16), provisions and other operating items.

exercises.q: Sort these items into the statement they belong to.
exercises.answer: The income statement holds revenue and expenses of the period; the balance sheet holds balances at a date; the cash flow statement holds cash movements, including capex and dividends, which never go through profit.
A prepaid expense is a right to a future service (asset); deferred revenue is a service still owed to a customer (liability); an accrued expense is a cost incurred but not yet invoiced (liability).

exercises.q: Put the income statement lines in order, from top to bottom.
exercises.answer: Revenue − cost of sales = gross profit; − operating expenses = EBIT; − net finance costs = profit before tax; − income tax = net income.

exercises.q: Match each ratio with its formula.
exercises.answer: ROE measures the return to shareholders; ROCE measures the return of the business whatever its financing; interest cover and net debt / EBITDA are what lenders read first.

exercises.q: Depreciation increases by 10 and the tax rate is 25 %. What happens to the company’s cash?
exercises.answer: Depreciation is not a cash payment, but it lowers taxable profit: tax falls by 2.5. Net income is down 7.5, the 10 of depreciation is added back, so operating cash flow rises by 2.5.

exercises.q: On 30 June your company delivers goods to a customer for 150, payable in 60 days. The goods cost 100 and were already in stock. Walk the sale through the statements at 30 June.

steps.text: What is the effect on the income statement (before tax)?

choices.label: Revenue +150, cost of sales +100, profit +50
choices.feedback: Right: the goods are delivered, so the performance obligation is satisfied and revenue is recognised now, with its cost.

choices.label: Nothing until the customer pays
choices.feedback: That is cash accounting. Under accruals (IFRS 15), revenue follows delivery, not payment.

choices.label: Revenue +150 only; the cost was booked when the stock was bought
choices.feedback: Buying stock creates an asset, not an expense. The cost reaches the income statement when the goods are sold.

steps.text: What is the effect on cash at 30 June?

choices.label: Cash +150
choices.feedback: The customer pays in 60 days: no cash has moved yet.

choices.label: No change
choices.feedback: Right: the sale creates a receivable; cash moves when the customer pays.

choices.label: Cash +50
choices.feedback: Profit is not cash: neither the sale nor the cost moved cash on 30 June.

steps.text: How does the indirect cash flow statement show it, and does the balance sheet balance?

choices.label: Net income +50, increase in receivables −150, decrease in inventories +100: operating cash 0. Assets +50 (receivables +150, inventories −100) = equity +50.
choices.feedback: Exactly: the working capital lines cancel the profit, and the balance sheet balances through retained earnings (ignoring tax).

choices.label: Net income +50 in operating cash flow, nothing else
choices.feedback: That would show 50 of cash that does not exist. The increase in receivables must be subtracted and the decrease in inventories added back.

choices.label: Receivables +150 under investing activities
choices.feedback: Trade receivables are working capital, so they stay in operating activities.

exercises.answer: Income statement: revenue 150, cost of sales 100, profit 50. Cash flow: 50 − 150 + 100 = 0. Balance sheet: receivables +150, inventories −100, so assets +50, matched by retained earnings +50.

exercises.q: Current assets are 480 and current liabilities 320. What is the current ratio?
exercises.answer: 480 / 320 = 1.5: the company holds 1.5 of short-term assets for each 1 of short-term debt. Check the quick ratio too: if most of the current assets are slow-moving stock, liquidity is weaker than it looks.

exercises.q: In B6, compute the EBITDA margin. Cost of sales and operating expenses are shown before depreciation and amortisation.
exercises.explain: EBITDA = revenue − cost of sales − operating expenses, all before D&A: 2,400 − 1,440 − 480 = 480, so the margin is 480 / 2,400 = 20 %. Subtracting B5 as well gives the EBIT margin (15 %), not EBITDA.

exercises.q: In B5, compute DSO (days sales outstanding).
exercises.explain: DSO = trade receivables / revenue × days: 1,200 / 7,300 × 365 = 60 days. Customers take two months to pay on average.

exercises.q: In C4, compute FY2025 ROE on average equity (the average of the FY2024 and FY2025 closing equity).
exercises.explain: ROE = net income / average equity = 90 / ((460 + 500) / 2) = 90 / 480 = 18.75 %. Average equity matches the profit of the whole year with the capital used during that year.

exercises.q: In B8, compute the cash conversion cycle in days (DSO + DIO − DPO), using B7 for the days in the year.
exercises.explain: DSO = 1,200 / 7,300 × 365 = 60, DIO = 720 / 4,380 × 365 = 60, DPO = 540 / 4,380 × 365 = 45, so the cycle is 60 + 60 − 45 = 75 days. Inventories and payables are divided by cost of sales, receivables by revenue.

exercises.q: A fast-growing client shows a net income of 2 million but keeps drawing on its overdraft. Explain to your manager how this is possible and what you would check.
exercises.answer: Profit is not cash. First, working capital: with growth, receivables and inventories grow before customers pay; I would compute DSO, DIO and DPO over several periods and the change in working capital in the cash flow statement. Second, capex: investment for growth is cash out now but reaches profit only through depreciation. Third, the quality of profit: revenue recognised early (long credit terms, bill-and-hold, aggressive IFRS 15 judgements), capitalised costs, or one-off gains. I would compare operating cash flow with EBITDA (cash conversion), look at free cash flow, read the notes on revenue and receivables (ageing, large customers, factoring) and check the debt maturities and covenants to see how long the overdraft can carry the growth.

exercises.q: In B8, compute the valeur ajoutée (value added) from this French (PCG) income statement.
rows: Cost of goods sold (coût d'achat des marchandises vendues)
Change in finished goods inventory (production stockée)
External consumption (consommations en provenance de tiers)
exercises.explain: Trading margin = 300 − 180 = 120; output for the year = 900 + 30 + 20 = 950 (stocked and capitalised production count as output even though they are not sold); value added = 120 + 950 − 520 = 550.

exercises.q: In B8, compute the EBE (excédent brut d’exploitation).
rows: Taxes other than income tax (impôts et taxes)
Depreciation and provisions (dotations aux amortissements et provisions)
exercises.explain: EBE = value added + operating subsidies − taxes other than income tax − personnel costs = 550 + 15 − 25 − 340 = 200. Depreciation and provisions come after EBE (they lead to the résultat d’exploitation) and finance costs after that, so B6 and B7 stay out.

exercises.q: In B8, compute the CAF (capacité d’autofinancement) with the additive method.
rows: Proceeds from asset disposals (produits de cession)
Net book value of assets sold (VNC des éléments cédés)
Investment subsidies released to income (quote-part des subventions d'investissement)
exercises.explain: Start from net income and remove everything that is not an operating cash flow: + charges not paid in cash (65), − write-backs (15), − disposal proceeds (40) + net book value of the assets sold (25) (the disposal gain is investing, not operations), − investment subsidies released to income (5). CAF = 90 + 65 − 15 − 40 + 25 − 5 = 120.

exercises.q: In B7, compute the FRNG (fonds de roulement net global) from this functional balance sheet in gross values.
rows: Accumulated depreciation and impairment (amortissements et dépréciations)
Provisions for risks and charges (provisions pour risques et charges)
Long-term borrowings (dettes financières à long terme)
exercises.explain: Stable resources = equity + accumulated depreciation and impairment + provisions + long-term borrowings = 620 + 280 + 40 + 360 = 1,300; stable uses = gross fixed assets 1,000; FRNG = 300. Working in net values (without the 280 on both sides) gives the same FRNG.

exercises.q: In B8, compute the trésorerie nette as FRNG − BFR in one formula.
rows: Tax and social security payables (dettes fiscales et sociales)
exercises.explain: BFR = inventories + operating receivables − operating payables = 180 + 260 + 20 − 150 − 70 = 240; trésorerie nette = 300 − 240 = 60. Identity check: on the balance sheet, cash at bank minus bank overdrafts must also give 60; if it does not, an item is in the wrong block (for example an overdraft counted as long-term debt).

exercises.q: Put the soldes intermédiaires de gestion (SIG) in the order of the PCG cascade, from top to bottom.
steps: Production de l’exercice (output for the year)
exercises.answer: Trading margin and output for the year, then value added (both minus external consumption), EBE (− taxes and personnel costs), operating result (− depreciation and provisions), RCAI (± financial result), the exceptional result, and net income (− employee profit-sharing and income tax).

exercises.q: A company has an FRNG of 200 and a BFR of 260. What is its trésorerie nette and what does it mean?
options: −60: part of the BFR is financed by short-term bank credit (overdrafts)
exercises.answer: Trésorerie nette = FRNG − BFR = 200 − 260 = −60: stable resources do not cover the whole operating cycle, so overdrafts or short-term lines finance the gap. That is common in growing or seasonal businesses and not insolvency, but it depends on the bank keeping those lines open: check the trend of the BFR in days of revenue and the size of the facilities.

interview.q: Walk me through the three financial statements.
interview.a: The income statement shows performance over a period: revenue minus costs, down to net income. The balance sheet shows, at one date, what the company owns (assets) and how it is financed (liabilities and equity), and assets always equal liabilities plus equity. The cash flow statement explains the change in cash over the period in operating, investing and financing activities. They link: net income starts the cash flow statement and feeds retained earnings, non-cash items and working capital changes reconcile profit to operating cash flow, and the change in cash ties to the balance sheet.

interview.q: Depreciation goes up by 10. Walk me through the three statements.
interview.a: Assuming a 25 % tax rate: on the income statement EBIT falls by 10, tax by 2.5, net income by 7.5. On the cash flow statement net income is down 7.5, depreciation adds back 10, so operating cash flow is up 2.5. On the balance sheet PP&E is down 10 and cash up 2.5, so assets fall by 7.5; retained earnings fall by 7.5, so liabilities plus equity also fall by 7.5. It balances.

interview.q: Can a profitable company go bankrupt?
interview.a: Yes, because companies fail when they cannot pay, not when they lose money. A profitable company can run out of cash if working capital absorbs it (customers pay late, stock builds up, typically during fast growth), if it invests heavily in capex, or if debt falls due and cannot be refinanced. That is why I look at operating cash flow, free cash flow, the cash conversion cycle and debt maturities, not only at profit.

interview.q: What is EBITDA and what are its limits?
interview.a: EBITDA is operating profit before depreciation and amortisation, so EBIT plus D&A. It is popular because it removes the effect of past investment and accounting choices on depreciation, and it is the base of leverage covenants like net debt / EBITDA. Its limits: it is not cash, since it ignores capex, working capital changes, interest and tax; it is not defined by IFRS or US GAAP, so companies adjust it differently; and under IFRS 16 it excludes lease costs, which flatters it compared with US GAAP operating leases. I always reconcile it to reported EBIT and look at cash conversion.

interview.q: Where do you see deferred revenue and why does it matter?
interview.a: Deferred revenue, or a contract liability, is on the balance sheet as a liability: the customer has paid but the company still owes the service, for example an annual software subscription paid upfront. It is released into revenue as the service is delivered, under IFRS 15 or ASC 606. It matters because it is cash received in advance, which funds the business, and growing deferred revenue is a sign of future revenue already contracted; a sudden fall can announce a slowdown before revenue shows it.

interview.q: How would you assess a company’s financial health in ten minutes?
interview.a: Revenue growth and margin trends over three years, compared with peers. Then cash: operating cash flow compared with EBITDA, free cash flow, and the working capital days. Then the balance sheet: net debt / EBITDA, interest cover, liquidity (cash plus undrawn credit lines against debt due within a year) and covenants. Then returns: ROCE against the cost of capital. Finally I read the auditor’s report and the notes on revenue, debt and provisions, and I list the questions I would ask management.

interview.q: What is the difference between ROE and ROCE, and which do you prefer?
interview.a: ROE is net income over average equity: the return to shareholders, which rises with leverage. ROCE is EBIT over capital employed (total assets minus current liabilities, or equity plus net debt): the return of the business itself, whatever its financing. To judge the quality of a business I prefer ROCE and compare it with the cost of capital; to understand shareholder returns I use ROE and break it down with DuPont into margin, asset turnover and leverage, so I can see whether a high ROE comes from performance or from debt.

interview.q: What is the difference between EBE and EBITDA?
interview.a: Both measure operating performance before depreciation, but EBE is defined by the French PCG: value added + operating subsidies − taxes other than income tax − personnel costs. It stops before provisions and other operating income and charges. EBITDA is not defined by any standard: each company defines it, usually as EBIT plus depreciation and amortisation, sometimes adjusted. The big practical gap is leases: under IFRS 16 rent is replaced by depreciation and interest, so it leaves EBITDA, while in French individual accounts rent stays an external charge inside EBE. When I compare the two, I reconcile them line by line: leases, provisions, other operating items and any adjustments.

interview.q: A client has a positive fonds de roulement but negative trésorerie nette. What does that tell you, and what do you check?
interview.a: Since trésorerie nette = FRNG − BFR, the BFR is larger than the fonds de roulement: stable resources finance all the fixed assets and part of the operating cycle, and overdrafts or short-term lines finance the rest. That is not insolvency, but it depends on the bank. I check the BFR in days of revenue over several years (is it growth, or slower customer payments and stock building?), the CAF and its trend, financial debt / CAF, the size and maturity of the short-term facilities, and seasonality, since a year-end balance sheet can be the best or worst point of the year. Remedies are on both sides: reduce the BFR (collection, stock, supplier terms) or raise stable resources (equity, medium-term loan).
